newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS-HK, CHINA ISSUERS LOOK TO YANKEES.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS-HK, CHINA ISSUERS LOOK TO YANKEES.

text.p: Inspired by the stunning success of the Hutchison Whampoa Ltd US$2 billion deal last month, Hong Kong and China issuers are looking at yankee bonds, bankers said on Tuesday.
Bankers expect at least three issues in the first two weeks of September, including a US$300 million 10-year 144a from Sung Hung Kai Properties Ltd.
Bankers said Merrill Lynch is mandated for Sun Hung Kai Properties deal, and J.P. Morgan was arranging a US$300 million issue for CITIC Pacific Ltd.
Merrill Lynch declined to comment on Sun Hung Kai.
Bankers said many local corporates were getting used to the idea of locking in longer term financing.
"It actually makes logical sense for some companies -- not all of them -- to go out long term because their asset base is so long term," a U.S. investment banker told Reuters.
"They're getting religion -- match long-term assets with long-term liabilities," he added.
In other news, Shanghai Pudong Development Bank plans to raise US$50 million through a 364-day floating rate certificate of deposit issue.
The issue will carry a coupon of 23.5 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate, and is expected to offer an all-in of 28.5 basis points.
One bank said the all-in was likely to be 28.5 basis points.
Arrangers are Chase Manhattan Asia (books), Fuji International Finance, HSBC Markets (books, publicity) and Standard Chartered (agent). It is expected later this month.
New World Development Co Ltd has mandated Sumitomo Bank, Societe Generale Asia, BA Asia, Deutsche Bank to arrange a HK$6 billion seven-year loan.
Bankers said the loan included a five-year put option.
In other news, reaction to Monday's rescue package by the International Monetary Fund and Asian central banks by commercial banks was muted.
Despite the rescue package, bankers said Thai banks would still have to pay top price in the market.
"Top Thai financial institutions would have to pay an enormous premium if we were to arrange a deal for them (now)," said one banker with a Japanese bank.
"And if we did, we would ask them for certain financial covenants," the banker added.
Bankers cited Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand (IFCT) as an example of the tougher structures.
IFCT issued a larger bond featuring credit clauses in late July, including a put exercisable if its rating fell below investment grade.
"That's the one problem -- that IFCT has set a market precedent. If such a good company has to put puts in to protect it, doesn't every borrower below them have to?" said one investment banker.
